title: What to do with your savings when interest rates drop
description: Strategies to protect your yield as the Federal Reserve cuts rates.
content:
For the last few years, savers have enjoyed a 'Golden Age' of cash, earning 5% in risk-free savings accounts. But interest rates are cyclical. When the Federal Reserve cuts rates to stimulate the economy, the yield on your High-Yield Savings Account (HYSA) will drop instantly. If you sit passively, your 5% return could become 2% very quickly. The key to maintaining income is **locking in duration**. You must move cash from variable-rate accounts (HYSA) to fixed-rate accounts (CDs/Bonds) *before* the cuts happen.

Key Takeaways

  • Reinvestment Risk: The risk that when your investment matures, you can only reinvest at a lower rate. Cash has maximum reinvestment risk.
  • Lock In Now: Buying a 5-Year CD or Treasury Note today guarantees you that rate for 5 years, even if the Fed cuts rates to zero next year.
  • Bond Price Appreciation: When rates fall, bond prices rise. Holding a bond fund (BND) can generate capital gains during rate cuts, offering a double benefit.
  • Don't Reach for Yield: Avoid buying risky Junk Bonds just to maintain 5%. Accept lower safe yields or take equity risk; don't mix them.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The Federal Reserve controls the 'Fed Funds Rate', which dictates HYSA yields. Markets are forward-looking; by the time the Fed *announces* a cut, the yields on 2-Year and 10-Year Treasuries have usually already dropped. Speed matters.

The Hierarchy of Duration

As rates fall, you want to own assets that locked in the old high rates.

1. Cash / HYSA (Worst)

Rate floats daily. If Fed cuts 0.50%, your bank cuts 0.50% next week. Zero protection.

2. Certificates of Deposit (Better)

Locks the rate for the term. A 5-Year CD at 4.5% is a gold mine if rates drop to 2%. You continue earning 4.5% until maturity.

3. Treasury Notes / Bond Funds (Best Total Return)

If you own a 10-Year Treasury paying 4.5% and market rates drop to 3.5%, your bond becomes more valuable. You can sell it for a profit (Capital Gain) OR hold it for the high income. Bond Funds (like BND) will see their share price rise.

The 'CD Ladder' Defense

  1. Audit Your Cash: Identify funds you won't need for >1 year.
  2. Buy Long-Term CDs: Instead of a 6-month CD, buy a 2-Year or 3-Year CD/Treasury. You are buying 'yield insurance'.
  3. Move to Bonds: If you were hiding in cash because '5% is good enough,' it's time to move back to a diversified Bond Fund (AGG/BND). You want to capture the price appreciation that occurs during rate cuts.
  4. Pay Down Debt: If savings rates drop to 3% but your mortgage is 6%, paying down the mortgage becomes mathematically superior again.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I buy stocks when rates drop?

Generally, yes. Lower rates are good for stock valuations (companies can borrow cheaper). However, if rates are dropping because of a Recession, stocks might fall first before rising.

What is a 'Call Risk'?

Some CDs and Bonds are 'Callable'. This means if rates drop, the bank can force-return your money and cancel the interest. Always buy 'Non-Callable' CDs to protect your yield.

Is 3% bad?

Historically, no. 3% is normal. 0% was the anomaly. 5% was the bonus. Adjust your expectations. Beating inflation is the only goal that matters.
